newsitem.title: TANZANIA: IMF welcomes Tanzania's tax cuts over mining.
newsitem.headline: IMF welcomes Tanzania's tax cuts over mining.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund welcomed on Tuesday Tanzania cutting mining industry taxes to boost investment but warned against undermining its revenue collection.
The tax review announced last week would boost an industry which is capital intensive with few quick returns, said IMF representative in Tanzania, Festus Osunsade.
"But the government must not overdo things, by giving a lot of tax incentives and undermining government revenue collection plans."

Imported mining equipment would be exempted from import duty, sales tax and excise duty for up to a year after the start of a mining operation, Energy and Minerals minister Abdallah Kigoda said last week.
"Thereafter investors will be subjected to import taxes tariffs that are not beyond five percent of the value of imported inputs for mining activities," Kigoda said.
He also abolished the export levy and stamp duty on proceeds of minerals sold abroad and authorised a depreciation allowance of 100 percent on all mining capital expenditure.
The measures to start July were aimed at boosting the mining sector's contribution to the country's economic growth.
Minerals contribute about 10 percent of export revenue which stands at $600 million a year, about 1.7 percent of Tanzania's gross domestic product, according to government statistics.
Osunsade cited an IMF study showing that tax incentives, exemptions and concessions listed in the proposed new investment law could cost $120 billion shillings ($197 million) a year.
"This is a fourth of Tanzania government's annual revenue. How does the country benefit from such an arrangement?" he said.
He said the biggest obstacle for investors in Tanzania was not tax but red tape in an East African country where it takes up to three months for a project application to be approved.
